Q: To get us started, where are you from? Where did you grow up and what was the place like?
A: I am from the United States. I was born in Texas originally. I moved around a lot and lived in many different places. Some of the noteworthy ones included Portland, Vancouver, San Francisco and Yakima.
Q: Thinking back, what kind of student were you in school?
A: I was a diligent student who always took challenging topics. I often studied topics outside of school as well. During my senior year of high school, I skipped from 2nd to 4th year Japanese while teaching myself 1st year Latin. During that year, I also completed a full international baccalaureate course load and learned some coding in basic. I helped any student who asked.
Q: Did you have a teacher or teachers that were influential? If so, why? What were they like?
A: I had many excellent teachers. One of my favorites taught philosophy at a high school level. He encouraged me a great deal and helped me get a better graphing calculator to learn programming on. This was in 1995, and I did not own a computer. I had to learn programming on a graphing calculator. I also had a very good math teacher who convinced our high school to offer a more advanced math class to the best students. I dabbled in a broad range of topics that helped in college.
Q: What was your favorite subject in school, and why?
A: I liked almost all subjects about equally, because all subjects offered different tools to obtain and understand information. I was best at verbal topics like writing and language and had the hardest time with math, but that made me look into applied mathematics in college rather than shying away from it.
Q: What was your least favorite subject in school, and why?
A: The only topic I remember actually disliking was political science. I felt the field of study was too new and undisciplined, and lacked good tools to determine what was going on. I took that in college and it felt like a waste of my time.
Q: Still thinking back, who were your heroes when you were young and why?
A: I did not have heroes. As a child, I was aware that everyone has flaws and limits, even people that we admire. Rather than striving to emulate anyone in particular, I tried to learn what I could from everyone without idolizing them.
Q: When you were little, what did you want to be when you grew up? And why?
A: As a very small boy, I wanted to be a paleontologist because I loved dinosaurs. The idea of going to different places and digging up dinosaur bones, then puzzling out what they were was very appealing to me at that age.
Q: What were your dreams and plans when you graduated from high school? What made you have those dreams or plans?
A: I didn't really have any. I have a major depressive disorder called dysthymia, which makes a person's mood low all the time. I joined the Army with the idea of using the GI Bill to pay for college, but washed out. I ended up doing technical support and later dispatching, and only finished college later in life.
Q: If you had complete freedom, what would your dream job be, and why?
A: I would still be a writer, it would just be nice to be a famous one maybe, so I had lots of money.
Q: How have your dreams and goals changed throughout your life?
A: When I was younger, I did not feel that I had much to live for. I was very alone and very sad. As I've gotten older, I have developed good relationships and a foundation to continue. I met my partner about 18 years ago now, and now I mostly worry about looking out for her.
Q: Shifting gears to your childhood, how would you describe the personalities of people in the family you grew up in? For example, what were your parents and/or siblings like?
A: I was raised by my mother. She divorced my father for abuse, and I don't remember him. She is brave and smart, but very eccentric. Speaks many languages, traveled many places. Doesn't do anything normal. She has always been very involved in local politics, including a failed run for mayor one time. My sister rebelled against the family's general eccentricity by being very normal and successful. My sister had a job and car and moved out at 16. She had 2 children and a white picket fence in her early 20s.
Q: How are you similar or different from your parents and/or siblings?
A: My sister and I have a lot in common: we're independent and self-directed. We're both very smart. However, our outlooks and goals in life are opposite. I became very austere and intellectual: I am a poor artist with few connections. She is very materially successful, raised children and has a strong career. I think that losing everything so many times as children taught us different things: I learned that I was all I had, and she learned she wanted more stable outside connections.
Q: How do you think your similarities and/or differences influenced your relationship with them?
A: We love each other very much, but are not very close. Our worlds are very different. I miss her a lot, but we just don't have much in common and was harder with covid because everybody had to isolate.
Q: What was the best part of your childhood?
A: The best part of my childhood was also the worst: moving around a lot. I got to see so many places and different kinds of people. It taught me that people are fundamentally the same everywhere, but do have differences we can learn from.
Q: What do you think were the worst parts of your childhood?
A: Also moving around a lot. I lost everything more times than I could count, and it was hard. A lot of my life has been shaped by the understanding that everything in life is temporary.

Q: To get us started, where are you from? Where did you grow up and what was the place like?
A: I am from South Florida, in a city called Pembroke Pines It was a nice city. The city was medium-sized, and it is very hot and extremely humid. But, it was a fun place to grow up in.
Q: Thinking back, what kind of student were you in school?
A: I was an excellent student. I did well on exams and was well-respected by both my peers and by my teachers.
Q: Did you have a teacher or teachers that were influential? If so, why? What were they like?
A: Yeah, I remember my 4th grade teacher most of all. She always made classes interesting and fostered a classroom where people could make friends and have lots of fun. She was very patient with us and I don't remember her ever getting angry at us.
Q: What was your favorite subject in school, and why?
A: It was definitely math. Most likely because I was the best in my class at it. We would have competitions both in class and school-wide, and I was always at the top.
Q: What was your least favorite subject in school, and why?
A: When I lived in Peru for a couple of years, we had to take dance lessons as a class - a "dance" class was a regular part of the schedule. I hated that because I am a very untalented dancer.
Q: Still thinking back, who were your heroes when you were young and why?
A: I don't remember having heroes in particular. Maybe superheroes like Spiderman when I was a little kid. Other than that, I would say my parents were people I aspired to be like when I grew up.
Q: When you were little, what did you want to be when you grew up? And why?
A: That very much depends on my age. When I was very little, I wanted to be a photographer, because that is what my dad does. He is a wedding photographer.
Q: What were your dreams and plans when you graduated from high school? What made you have those dreams or plans?
A: At that time, my plan was to pursue a career in finance, probably as an investment banker. My mindset was that in such a career I would be able to make a lot of money and this would give me freedom to support my family and do what I want.
Q: If you had complete freedom, what would your dream job be, and why?
A: I want to be an academic who does research in social psychology as well as a couples' therapist. I am on my way now towards becoming an academic. Becoming a therapist is something I'd need to get a license for afterwards - that is the plan!
Q: How have your dreams and goals changed throughout your life?
A: I have placed much less emphasis on money and have chosen to make my life more suitable to a balanced lifestyle, where I can have more time for spending with others I care about. This meant getting out of the track I was on to getting a finance job and choosing a much less lucrative career in academia.
Q: Shifting gears to your childhood, how would you describe the personalities of people in the family you grew up in? For example, what were your parents and/or siblings like?
A: My brother is much more outgoing than me, but he was less of a troublemaker. My mom was strict and would push me to be my best self, but also matched every bit of strictness with love and care. My dad was a good dad and made time to spend time and play with me.
Q: How are you similar or different from your parents and/or siblings?
A: I am very similar to my mom in that we are both stubborn and fight for our beliefs very strongly. We are resilient and don't back away from an argument. I am different from my mom in that I am more intellectually oriented than her. She also enjoys things that I don't, such as spending time at the beach and waking up early to go see sunrises.
Q: How do you think your similarities and/or differences influenced your relationship with them?
A: Our similarities are very fun to point out, but it has resulted in our relationship being characterized by a lot of argumentation. Not always of a serious or bad kind, but definitely not as smooth as her relationship with my brother. Our differences also cause some contention, as we struggle to find things we enjoy doing together. Still, she is an amazing mother and I think our relationship overall is very strong!
Q: What was the best part of your childhood?
A: My mom being a reliable source of affection and understanding, as well as a source of motivation to do better was the best part, because it has most directly impacted who I am today.
Q: What do you think were the worst parts of your childhood?
A: I had to move to Peru when I was nine, and being separated from the friends I had made up until that point was very difficult.
Q: Switching gears a little bit, what was your first paid job? How old were you then? (If this is not applicable to you, then please put 'NA')
A: My first paid job was when I was 20 - I was paid to be a writing tutor for fellow undergraduate students. I would help them brainstorm or edit papers on a variety of subjects.
Q: What other jobs have you had? (If this is not applicable to you, then please put 'NA')
A: I have worked at my university's library, attaining a supervisory role shortly after. I was briefly a college admissions tutor of sorts, but that didn't work out.
Q: What do you do now for a living? And why did you choose it?
A: I am currently about to graduate with my bachelor's in psychology, and will be a doctoral student in a couple of months. I chose it because doing research in psychology is my passion, and getting paid to do something I am passionate about sounds ideal.
Q: Please describe your typical work day.
A:  On days I have class, I wake up around 9 am, get ready for the day and go to my first class at 10. I have classes back to back, with a short lunch break, until 3:30. Then I work for an hour before getting dinner and going to the gym. I eat again afterwards, then do work for the rest of the night until around 1 or two hours before I go to bed. I approach my work with diligence and discipline, as this is required for me to do well.
Q: What is the best and worst part of your current work?
A: I go to a top university, so being able to interact with amazing fellow students and professors, and having a wide variety of opportunities to learn and grow as a person. I am busy most of the time and have little time to spend on doing other hobbies I would like to spend time on.
Q: Did you serve in the military? Please tell us about that experience, what was the best and worst part of it?
A: No, I have never served in the military and don't intend to do so.
Q: Moving on, what are your adult friendships like?
A: I have only a few friendships, but they are very deep and rewarding. I have a best friend I can tell anything to and always rely on, and he knows that I can serve that role for him as well.
Q: How are your adult friendships different from your childhood friendships?
A: I think they are different in that my adult friendships are grounded on more serious commonalities, such as in principles we hold about how to live our lives. When we are children, we don't have that wisdom.
Q: What are your strongest qualities as a friend? In other words, what makes you a great friend to have?
A: I think I always make time for my friends no matter how busy I am. I think I am a good listener. I am reliable and understand when others are busy and can't make time for the friendship.
Q: What about your weakest qualities in friendships? In other words, what do you struggle with when you are trying to be a friend to someone?

A: I have been able to achieve great things without being particularly advantaged. I have worked hard and made it to a top university, and now have the opportunity to do what I want as a career and be well positioned to excel at it.

Q: To get us started, where are you from? Where did you grow up and what was the place like?
A: i was born in Indiana, but only lived there until i was 5. my dad got a job in Minneapolis, so we moved there, and i lived there until high school. after my parents divorced, my mom moved to Salt Lake City, and i followed her. i lived there for about twenty years, and now i live in Boston. usually i think of myself as being from both Indiana and Salt Lake City. that is kind of a complicated question given how much we moved, but i tend to think of Minneapolis as where i did most of my growing up. i loved bicycling around the lakes with my parents, and swimming in the lake closest to us. i spent a lot of time at the local library, and it was always a treat to visit the Mississippi river and see the locks and dams.
Q: Thinking back, what kind of student were you in school?
A: when i was younger, i was always eager to learn anything, and to show off my knowledge, so i got really good grades and was frequently in advanced classes. but when my parents got divorced i fell into a deep depression, so my middle school and high school years were much more difficult. i still enjoyed learning, but didn't care about doing homework, so my grades weren't very good.
Q: Did you have a teacher or teachers that were influential? If so, why? What were they like?
A: my most influential teacher was in college. she taught a required ethics for engineers class. i was already pretty convinced that the ethics of their work was something engineers of all sorts had to take seriously, so i really fell in love with her classes, and took every one she offered even if it wasn't required. she really taught me how to think more deeply about experiences outside my own, and i would not be the person i am today without her.
Q: What was your favorite subject in school, and why?
A: honestly i loved all of them, especially when i was younger. in high school math started to get too abstract without having any idea of what it was good for so i became less interested, and i started to be more into the humanities. i always loved to read, so anything that gave me the chance to read more and think and talk about what i was reading was great.
Q: What was your least favorite subject in school, and why?
A: i really wanted to like physics, but i didn't understand it *at all*. i don't actually know what i was expecting it to be, but whatever it actually was wasn't that expectation, and i hated every moment of it.
Q: Still thinking back, who were your heroes when you were young and why?
A: Kirby Puckett was the big name in the Minnesota Twins baseball team at the time, which i really enjoyed watching. and i idolized any astronaut, and anyone who was on Star Trek!
Q: When you were little, what did you want to be when you grew up? And why?
A: an astronaut, a paleontologist, occasionally a rock star. i loved space, and dinosaurs, and music. it turns out i had no desire to actually do any of the things required to be any of those, though, and that's fine.
Q: What were your dreams and plans when you graduated from high school? What made you have those dreams or plans?
A: my girlfriend and i were going to move to Minneapolis because we both wanted to get the hell out of Salt Lake, and that's where i'd lived before (and visited during school breaks, since my dad still lived there). we did move there for the summer, and lived with my dad, but we couldn't actually find enough work to be able to move out. the stress of that broke up our relationship, and we eventually both moved back to Salt Lake City, separately. after that i didn't really have any dreams or plans for a long time, i was just trying to get by.
Q: If you had complete freedom, what would your dream job be, and why?
A: i'd be the weird lady who lives on the edge of town that people come to when they need help, and i could make a potion or some sort of charm to fix their problem. i don't want to have a normal life, and i'm blessed to not have to as it is.
Q: How have your dreams and goals changed throughout your life?
A: they've mostly become smaller. i used to dream of being famous, or travelling the world, and now i mostly just want to be left in peace and be able to live my life, and try to make the world a slightly better place than it was.
Q: Shifting gears to your childhood, how would you describe the personalities of people in the family you grew up in? For example, what were your parents and/or siblings like?
A: my parents always nurtured my curiosity about the world, and were curious about it themselves. my dad is much more rationalistic and scientific, and my mom much more inclined towards the mystical, but for both of them i think it stems from a love of all life and curiosity about how the world works. they're both very kind people, and really funny. i don't have any siblings.
Q: How are you similar or different from your parents and/or siblings?
A: my facial features are very similar to my dad's, and our laugh is the same, and so is a lot of our body language. it's uncanny. but i think my personality is much more like my mom.
Q: How do you think your similarities and/or differences influenced your relationship with them?
A: after my parents divorced, i always found living with my dad very difficult. we were always at odds. now that we live apart, we're great friends. i was, admittedly, a pretty messed up teenager, and i don't envy either of my parents having to put up with me, but they managed it with as much grace as they could. i always got along better with my mom when living with her, but her house was really small and neither of us ever really had enough space to fully be ourselves, so it still wasn't a ton of fun. i'm a lot closer with her now that i don't live apart, too.
Q: What was the best part of your childhood?
A: i think just growing up while the internet was still a novelty. cell phones weren't common yet, and i could just be a kid without constantly being watched. obviously my parents tried to keep me safe, but that looked a lot different in the 80s and 90s than it does now. i could just go off and spend the day with my friends and no one would know where we were or what we were doing.
Q: What do you think were the worst parts of your childhood?
A: my parents divorce. it really messed me up throughout my teens, and i didn't really recover from that until after i'd  moved out and been living on my own for a years and i was able to start relating to my parents as an adult.
Q: Switching gears a little bit, what was your first paid job? How old were you then? (If this is not applicable to you, then please put 'NA')
A: i was a bagger at the grocery store near my house when i was 15 or 16.
Q: What other jobs have you had? (If this is not applicable to you, then please put 'NA')
A: i've worked at a few fast food restaurants, doing almost everything there; i worked at a thrift store, mostly as a cashier, i worked for the USPS, transcribing addresses on letters the machines couldn't process, i've worked in call centers, one of which developed into a software testing job that i stayed at for longer than i've worked anywhere else. after i moved to Boston i worked at a clothing store, but then my joints started to hurt too much from that. now i'm a housewife.
Q: What do you do now for a living? And why did you choose it?
A: like i said, i'm a housewife. i couldn't keep working retail, and i don't have any formal training in anything. all of my better jobs i've gotten by knowing people that work there, and i've learned how to do the job on the fly. but i moved to Boston and don't have contacts who can get me a job that can match my capabilities. my partner makes enough that she can pay our bills, so i do the cooking and cleaning. i didn't so much choose it as it just became the easiest arrangement for both of us. i do surveys on prolific for spending money.
Q: Please describe your typical work day.
A:  i wake up, pray, and make breakfast for me and my partner. then she starts work (she works for home), and i usually do some dishes, then relax at my computer for a while. if there are any surveys on prolific available i'll do them, otherwise i might play video games or just chat with my friends. throughout the day when i have the energy i try to get up and do other stuff as needed, until it's time to make dinner. after that my partner and i like to spend time together.
Q: What is the best and worst part of your current work?
A: it's really gratifying to try cooking something new for dinner and have my partner really like it! i don't have the physical ability to do all the cleaning that needs to happen, so there's always too much clutter around and nothing is as clean as i'd like it to be.
Q: Did you serve in the military? Please tell us about that experience, what was the best and worst part of it?
A: i didn't. i don't think there's anything else i want to add.
Q: Moving on, what are your adult friendships like?
A: these days, they're mostly online. i used to have a closer group local to me, but rising rents have pushed us all further away. and then the pandemic happened, so we couldn't meet up in person anyway. so i'm in a couple of knitting groups that originally met in person but are now online. and of course i can't see my friends from Salt Lake City in person either, so we mostly talk through facebook. i've made a lot of friends through twitter, and talk to people there or on other platforms. sometimes i get together with people locally, but it's pretty rare.
Q: How are your adult friendships different from your childhood friendships?
A: well, they're much more intentional. my childhood friendships were defined primarily on who was around me, either in my neighborhood or who i went to school with. i was lucky to have a couple of really good friends, but i suppose not everyone was. but as an adult, most of my friendships are based around some sort of shared interests, not physical proximity. i've never met quite a lot of people i'm very close to, and unfortunately probably never will meet many of them.
Q: What are your strongest qualities as a friend? In other words, what makes you a great friend to have?
A: i think i'm really loyal, and i'm always happy to help a friend who needs something, in whatever ways i can. i'm a good listener, and i'm pretty funny, too!
Q: What about your weakest qualities in friendships? In other words, what do you struggle with when you are trying to be a friend to someone?
A: i'm very bad at reaching out when i'm hurting, and honestly just in general. the people i'm friends with have to be ok with sometimes not talking for weeks or months, and they all are-- otherwise the friendship wouldn't actually have lasted.
Q: Moving onto more general questions, when thinking about your life in general, what are you most proud of?
A: i guess that i was able to transition. i knew i was trans in my teens, but didn't have the support i needed to do anything about it, so i just pushed those feelings deep, deep down. it wasn't until my early thirties that they started to come back, and this time i listened to them and was able to follow through on them, and start hormones.
Q: What hobbies or other interests do you have?
A: i like knitting, listening to music, playing video games, building models, reading, and dancing. i can't dance as much as i used to, though, because i risk injuring myself. it really sucks! game
Q: What things frighten you now?
A:  the increasingly outwardly fascist republic party trying to eliminate trans and disabled people, and the democrats not pushing back against it with nearly as much force as is required to actually stop that from happening.
Q: What were some things that frightened you most as a child?
A: i was scared of heights, and bugs. heights still give me the heebie jeebies, but i've become much more chill about the existence of bugs.
Q: What are the three biggest news events that have occurred in your lifetime?
A: the fall of the berlin wall and the soviet union; the invention of the internet, and 9/11.
Q: If you had the power to solve one and only one problem in the world, what would it be, and why?
A: i would eradicate fascism forever. i don't know how that's even possible, but it's the biggest threat to everyone and everything i hold dear.
Q: Tell me about a time when you did not know if you would make it. How did you overcome that challenge?
A: i went to a weird high school, that sent us on a lot of camping trips. my very first one, at the beginning of my first year, was a ten day backpacking trip in southern Utah. i didn't like the heat, so i was pretty miserable being in the desert, and was praying for rain. so one day, after descending a very deep canyon (which since i was afraid of heights  was very stressful! i only managed that part because a friend lent me his walkman so i could focus on the music instead), it started to rain. the rain quickly turned into flash flooding. we were able to find an overhang to shelter under, and the main path through the canyon was low enough that the floodwaters didn't reach us-- but if we hadn't had that shelter, we very well all could have drowned. i didn't really do anything special, i was absolutely terrified, and really i'm just lucky that we had any shelter, and the flooding wasn't worse

Q: To get us started, where are you from? Where did you grow up and what was the place like?

Q: Thinking back, what kind of student were you in school?

Q: Did you have a teacher or teachers that were influential? If so, why? What were they like?
A: Not really.  I would be hard pressed to even remember any of my teachers names.  Granted that I am 42 and that was a LONG time ago.
Q: What was your favorite subject in school, and why?
A: Thats difficult to answer.  I really enjoyed the computer classes but back then they weren't particularly advanced.  I remember in grade school they still  had us learning to type on typewriters!  I think my favorite subject was math.  It came very easily for me and made a lot of sense in my head.  I preferred that there was an actual, specific right answer to problems versus writing assignments or art assignments where the grading seemed much more subjective.
Q: What was your least favorite subject in school, and why?
A: Math was my favorite subject because it was very easy for me and I liked that the answers were specific.
Q: Still thinking back, who were your heroes when you were young and why?

Q: When you were little, what did you want to be when you grew up? And why?

He surrounded me with technology growing up and in that time period there were a LOT of nascent technologies.  It led me down the path of Computer Science.
Q: What were your dreams and plans when you graduated from high school? What made you have those dreams or plans?
A: I actually struggled quite a bit after graduating high school, I spent the summer in Europe which was great but waited until the last possible minute to accept my college admission. I was undeclared for several years.  Eventually, I wound up exactly on the path I had intended before, computer science.
Q: If you had complete freedom, what would your dream job be, and why?
A: Honestly, I would LOVE to work in the video game industry.  There is a mixture of technology, math, art, and creativity that I find really appealing.
Q: How have your dreams and goals changed throughout your life?
A: It becomes less about owning specific things or tangible assets and moves to more abstract things.  Now I am just searching for happiness and safety for myself, my dog and my friends.  If I don't have a mansion or a super sports car it is no longer important.
Q: Shifting gears to your childhood, how would you describe the personalities of people in the family you grew up in? For example, what were your parents and/or siblings like?

Q: How are you similar or different from your parents and/or siblings?
A: As I said above, I was not much like my sister though in a lot of ways our personalites have swapped so that we are still different now.  Adult me and young her would get along better just as Adult her and young me would.  My parents I got a little bit of each of them so I was able to get along with both.   My mom and I could be more creative and my dad and I could be more analytical.
Q: How do you think your similarities and/or differences influenced your relationship with them?
A: It brought us closer together.  My family was pretty close knit for sure.
Q: What was the best part of your childhood?
A: I think I was lucky to be a child when I was compared to nowadays.  We could ride our bikes all day and go miles away without supervision.  We could truly go on our own adventures and get in to all kinds of trouble.  Children today are incredibly sheltered and coddled.
Q: What do you think were the worst parts of your childhood?
A: Our family was pretty middle class but at times we were definitely lower middle class.  At times we struggled with money and not being able to afford things. Q: What other jobs have you had? (If this is not applicable to you, then please put 'NA')

Q: What do you do now for a living? And why did you choose it?

More of a I need to pay my bills in order to live job.  It has since became a financial boon and a long term position for me though.
Q: Please describe your typical work day.

Q: What is the best and worst part of your current work?

A: I would probably say work achievements though it would be difficult to narrow it down.

I am not doing the experiments on a daily basis anymore, but I enjoy leading the direction of the research, and I enjoy mentoring others.  I enjoy what I do.
Q: What is the best and worst part of your current work?
A: I love making new discoveries.  The opportunity to learn something that no one has ever known and then be able to present it at conferences and publish it is very exciting. It can be very stressful.  Success is dependent on publishing and getting grant funding.  I have dealt with many rejected papers and grant applications, and that can sometimes be hard to take.
Q: Did you serve in the military? Please tell us about that experience, what was the best and worst part of it?
A: I did not serve in the military.
Q: Moving on, what are your adult friendships like?
A: My best friend is my wife.  After that, I have a few friends through work and social activities.  I enjoy hanging out with those people, and we all support each other when needed.
Q: How are your adult friendships different from your childhood friendships?
A: My adult friendships are built upon a support system.  My friends are the people who are looking out for me, and I in turn am looking out for them.  My childhood friendships were based on proximity - who was around to play with and hang out with.  I'm not really in regular contact with any of my childhood friends anymore.
Q: What are your strongest qualities as a friend? In other words, what makes you a great friend to have?
A: I'm a good listener and strive to be supportive of my friends when they need someone.  I find that people often want to talk to me when they are struggling with something.  I think they value my time and my input.
Q: What about your weakest qualities in friendships? In other words, what do you struggle with when you are trying to be a friend to someone?
A: I don't really know.  We're all human and are not perfect.  I have flaws, but so does everyone else.  There's nothing that comes to mind specifically.
Q: Moving onto more general questions, when thinking about your life in general, what are you most proud of?
A: Probably my career.  I have worked very hard at my career.
Q: What hobbies or other interests do you have?
A: My hobbies are dancing, golf, pub trivia, and songwriting. 
Q: What things frighten you now?
A:  Getting old.  I worry about what my health will be when I age, and I worry about what finances will look like during retirement.  I have watched family members get old and struggle in every way, and it doesn't look fun.
Q: What were some things that frightened you most as a child?
A: Water.  I never learned how to swim, and I was very afraid of going into the water or getting on a boat.  I still don't like boats.
Q: What are the three biggest news events that have occurred in your lifetime?
A: Definitely 9/11.  I was in graduate school just outside New York City and remember everything about that day vividly.  I also remember the space shuttle Challenger exploding.  I was in middle school, and they brought the entire school together to tell us about the tragedy.  The third would be the COVID-19 pandemic.  That was a major shift in lifestyle for a period that everyone had to endure.
Q: If you had the power to solve one and only one problem in the world, what would it be, and why?
A: That's a tough question, but as a research scientist studying genetics, the clear answer that comes to mind is the ability to treat and cure genetic diseases.  Even the rare diseases impact a lot of people and families, and they can be devastating.  I hope that my research will at least make a small impact, but I know I'm only one person, and it will be small.  If I had the power to do more, I would definitely like to see those diseases eradicated.
Q: Tell me about a time when you did not know if you would make it. How did you overcome that challenge?
A: As I mentioned earlier, I have always had a fear of boats.  I was on a ferry once when the fire alarm went off.  I remember being very frightened and thinking that I might die on that boat.
